activities.caption: pair each design with its price
activities.name: rmDesignMatch

config.prompt: Six ways to collect evidence — pair each design (and variable) with its trade:

pairs.right: realism bought with noise, in schools, streets and hospitals
exploits events the researcher could not arrange — random assignment sacrificed, cause and effect murkier
what is measured while everything else is held still

config.why: Only randomised experiments establish cause — manipulate one variable, measure another, hold everything else still. Every other design trades that certainty for access.

config.prompt: Directional or non-directional? File each hypothesis statement:

items.label: sleep-deprived participants will recall fewer words
prior research already points that way
predicts a difference without saying which way
used when the literature gives no basis for a direction

config.why: A hypothesis must be falsifiable — state what result would prove it wrong (Popper's demand). An aim states what the study investigates; the hypothesis predicts.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — an operationalisation briefing
activities.name: rmOperSpot

config.prompt: One line of this operationalisation briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: 'Stress' becomes salivary cortisol, heart rate, or a score on a validated questionnaire.
'Memory' becomes number of words recalled from a 20-word list after 10 minutes.
Vague measures produce vague science; precise measures produce precise and contestable science.
Blend several measures and let the construct mean whatever the results need.
config.correction: Pick one, define it, and accept that you have thereby chosen one interpretation of the concept — which is why good papers defend theirs explicitly.
config.why: Which interpretation you chose is part of the finding — vague measures produce vague science.

activities.anchor: Any variable other than the IV that systematically affects
activities.caption: true or false — the war on confounds
activities.name: rmConfoundJudge

statements.s: Rosenthal and Fode's students told their rats were 'bright' recorded better maze times than students told their rats were 'dull' — and the rats were randomly assigned and identical.
statements.why: Investigator effects: the experimenter's expectations leaking into results.

statements.s: Demand characteristics are participants guessing the hypothesis and playing along.
statements.why: Which is why covert watching avoids them and blinding defuses them.

statements.s: A confound is a systematic influence on the dependent variable that is not the independent variable.
statements.why: Participant variables, situational variables, demand characteristics and investigator effects are all sources.

statements.s: Investigator effects can be eliminated simply by running larger samples.
statements.why: Blinding and standardisation are the counters — sample size changes precision, not leakage.

activities.caption: pair each statistic with its property
activities.name: rmStatsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each descriptive statistic with its property:

pairs.right: the average — sensitive to extreme scores
the middle score — robust to outliers
the most frequent score — the only option for nominal data
how tightly scores cluster around the mean

config.why: Two groups can share a mean and differ completely in variability — reporting central tendency and spread together is mandatory in honest work.

activities.anchor: could this pattern be a fluke of sampling
activities.caption: fill the significance reading
activities.name: rmPvalCloze

config.text: A significance test yields a p-value — by convention p under %%0%% counts as statistically significant, but read it correctly: it is evidence against the %%1%% hypothesis, not proof of yours, and it says nothing about how big the effect is.
config.hint: One blank is the conventional threshold; the other names the hypothesis being tested.

activities.anchor: Psychological research runs on people's trust
activities.caption: walk the ethics review
activities.name: rmEthicsBranch

config.root: You propose to study whether people conform under group pressure. The hard cases are real — walk the justification.

start.text: Your design needs deception: participants cannot know the true aim in advance. What do the professional codes require?

choices.label: Deceive freely — the findings justify it
choices.feedback: Deception is permitted only when unavoidable and trivial — and a full debrief must reveal anything withheld.

choices.label: Deceive only because it is unavoidable and trivial, then debrief fully
choices.feedback: That is the floor the codes set: minimal deception plus full disclosure afterwards.

review.text: The protocol now goes to the ethics committee before any data are collected. What do they weigh?

choices.label: Scientific value against participant burden
choices.feedback: Informed consent, protection from harm, right to withdraw without penalty, confidentiality, debrief — the non-negotiables sit on the same scale.

choices.label: Only the scientific value
choices.feedback: Participant burden weighs equally — consent, withdrawal, confidentiality and debrief are not optional extras.

approve.text: Approved, with the trade-off justified openly: consent, withdrawal without penalty, confidentiality, and a debrief revealing anything withheld.

config.why: Milgram's obedience experiments remain the boundary marker the codes were written against; the codes do not answer the hard cases — they force the researcher to justify the trade-off openly.

activities.caption: scrub the dates of the reckoning
activities.name: rmAuditTimeline

events.title: Fisher's publishing bar
events.text: Ronald Fisher sets 0.05 as a rough publishing bar — a century of treating it as a magic threshold follows.

events.title: Milgram's obedience experiments
events.text: Participants deceived into believing they delivered dangerous shocks — the boundary marker the codes were written against.

events.title: Rosenthal and Fode
events.text: Students told their rats were 'bright' record better maze times than students told 'dull' — the rats were randomly assigned and identical.

events.title: WEIRD samples
events.text: Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan document that the typical psychology participant is a statistical outlier of humanity.

events.title: The audit stings
events.text: The Open Science Collaboration reruns 100 famous studies; the original 'significant' result reproduces in about 36% of them.
